Neonatal Mottled skate (Beringraja pulchra) emerge from their egg cases at a modest total length of approximately 9.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 9.5 centimeters], a size consistent with the relatively small offspring typical of many oviparous skates. This length at birth marks the transition from a yolk-dependent embryo to an actively foraging neonate, a critical period of high mortality risk. Growth during the initial months is rapid, driven by the abundant benthic invertebrate prey available in the coastal habitats this species occupies. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C], the period from oviposition to emergence has been estimated at roughly 153 days [ab = roughly 153 days], reflecting the protracted embryonic development characteristic of many rajiform species. This relatively long incubation period, coupled with the small body size at hatching, suggests a life-history strategy favoring high early investment in yolk resources rather than rapid exit from the egg case. Additional observations indicate that the duration of the embryonic phase may vary with temperature fluctuations in the wild, potentially extending the incubation period by several weeks under cooler conditions. Such plasticity in developmental timing is a known adaptive feature among temperate skates.

As Beringraja pulchra progresses through its juvenile phase, sexual differentiation becomes apparent in the growth trajectories of males and females. Females achieve reproductive maturity at a notably larger body size, with puberty occurring at approximately 69 centimeters [Lp = approximately 69 centimeters] total length, whereas males attain sexual maturity at a considerably smaller size of about 47 centimeters [Lp = about 47 centimeters] total length. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in size at maturation is common among elasmobranchs and is thought to reflect the greater energetic demands of egg production and gestation in females relative to the production of spermatophores in males. Field surveys and captive observations indicate that the total length at which 50% of individuals are reproductively active aligns well with these values, although some geographic variation has been noted. Juvenile skates below these thresholds are typically excluded from breeding aggregations. The implications of this dimorphism for population dynamics are significant, as larger females contribute disproportionately to reproductive output.

The maximum reported longevity for Beringraja pulchra is 26 years [am = 26 years] when maintained at 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C], a lifespan that places it among the longer-lived members of the Rajidae. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a correspondingly large ultimate total length, with adults reaching up to 115 centimeters [Li = up to 115 centimeters] total length. Such a substantial body size, combined with a slow growth rate and late maturation, makes the species inherently vulnerable to overexploitation. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this maximum length has been estimated at approximately 14,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 14,700 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for the species. This large adult mass supports a relatively low metabolic rate per unit body weight, a trait shared with other demersal elasmobranchs. Comparative data from the same genus suggest that even slight increases in fishing mortality can drastically reduce the average age of the population, undermining reproductive potential over time.

Reproductive output in the Mottled skate is highly seasonal and strongly influenced by water temperature. At a stable thermal regime of 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C], females typically produce between one and two egg cases per oviposition event [N_R_i = between one and two egg cases per oviposition event], with a single oviposition event occurring approximately every 5 to 7 days during the peak breeding season. Over the course of a full annual cycle, an individual female may complete as many as 120 oviposition events [F_R_i = annual cycle, an individual female may complete as many as 120 oviposition events], resulting in an annual fecundity that ranges from 98 to 556 eggs per year. This remarkable inter-individual variation reflects differences in female body condition, prey availability, and the duration of the breeding season across the species' range. The daily reproductive rate implied by combining a typical clutch size of approximately 1.5 eggs with a frequency of one event every six days underscores the species' capacity for sustained, if intermittent, reproductive effort. Field studies further indicate that egg case deposition sites are often shared among multiple females, suggesting a degree of communal nesting that may enhance survival through predator dilution.

The conservation status of Beringraja pulchra is a growing concern, given its life-history traits of relatively slow growth, late maturation, and limited annual fecundity. The substantial disparity between the total length at puberty for females, measured at 69 centimeters [Lp = 69 centimeters], and the ultimate length of 115 centimeters [Li = 115 centimeters] means that individuals spend many years in a pre-reproductive juvenile state, accumulating biomass before first reproduction. Maximum recorded adult body mass of 14,700 grams [Wwi = 14,700 grams] is achieved only after decades of steady growth. Combined with the documented maximum lifespan of 26 years [am = 26 years] at 16.8 °C [T = 16.8 °C], these parameters suggest that even moderate levels of fishing mortality can severely depress population growth rates. Fisheries management for this species should therefore prioritize the protection of large, mature females to sustain reproductive output and population resilience, while also considering the role of marine protected areas in safeguarding critical nursery and spawning habitats.
